title: Insert & query across relationships
summary: Write rows that respect FKs, then JOIN / include to read graphs.

example.code: SELECT m.title, p.name FROM lab_magazines m JOIN lab_publishers p ON p.id = m.publisher_id;
example.sql: SELECT m.title, p.name FROM lab_magazines m JOIN lab_publishers p ON p.id = m.publisher_id;

exercise.prompt: Create both tables, insert 2 publishers + 3 magazines, then SELECT title + publisher name with a JOIN.
exercise.hint: JOIN lab_l10_publishers p ON p.id = m.publisher_id

wrongSolutions.label: SELECT without inserting rows
cross join (no ON) — every magazine paired with every publisher

data.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM lab_l10_magazines m JOIN lab_l10_publishers p ON p.id = m.publisher_id
data.message: Insert 3 magazines that belong to publishers (and commit) — the JOIN must find them.

stdout.message: SELECT title and publisher name, joined.

body:
Write rows that respect FKs, then JOIN / include to read graphs.

Why it matters: Schema without queries is incomplete. Inserts must satisfy FKs; reads use JOINs (or ORM include) to reassemble the relationship graph you modeled.

SQL ↔ ORM: SQL JOIN ↔ SQLAlchemy selectinload/joinedload ↔ Prisma include/select.
why: Schema without queries is incomplete. Inserts must satisfy FKs; reads use JOINs (or ORM include) to reassemble the relationship graph you modeled.
objectives: Insert parent before child when FKs are required.
Read across a relationship with JOIN or ORM navigation.
pitfalls: Selecting only one table and wondering where related fields went.
mappingNotes: SQL JOIN ↔ SQLAlchemy selectinload/joinedload ↔ Prisma include/select.
teachAlong: Cause: data is normalized across tables.
Effect: JOIN/include reconstitutes the object graph.
Validate: row counts and FK values match your intent.
